issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
The event that broke Kaimana happened on a late autumn afternoon, three years ago, when he was still working as a nanny for the Okada family in Honolulu. He had been with them for six years, caring for their two young daughters, Leilani and Malia, since they were infants. On that day, he had taken them to the beach park near their home. Malia, then four, had wandered toward the water while he was helping Leilani with her sandals. He heard the scream, turned, and saw her caught in a rip current, her small arms flailing. He ran in, but the current was too strong, and by the time lifeguards pulled her out, she was gone. Kaimana held her on the sand, her body limp and cold, and he remembers the sound of her mother’s wail when she arrived—a sound that now plays in his head without warning, high and thin, cutting through whatever he is doing.

In the months that followed, Kaimana found he could not talk about what happened. When his sister asked him to describe the afternoon, he started the sentence three times and each time lost the thread, the words dissolving into a thick grief that rose in his chest and stopped his breath. He would sit in silence, his hands trembling, while the sound of that wail filled his ears. He came to believe that his inability to finish the story was proof of something broken inside him—that he was weak, fundamentally, and that a strong man would have been able to save Malia or at least tell the story without falling apart. This belief that he was weak became a lens through which he saw everything. When he caught sight of a child’s small hand gripping a shopping cart handle, or a toddler’s bare foot in the sand, his stomach would clench and his mind would flood with images of Malia’s body, and he would think, *There it is again—you can’t even handle a hand without crumbling.*

The grief on recall was overwhelming. Every memory of Malia—her laugh, the way she said his name, the feel of her small hand in his—came wrapped in a fresh wave of loss so acute that he would sometimes find himself weeping on the kitchen floor, unable to move. And each time the grief hit, it confirmed what he already believed: that he was not a person anymore, just a hollow thing that felt pain. He had become an object that memories happened to, not a man who could act. This feeling of dehumanization grew stronger every time he failed to protect himself from a trigger, which was often. He stopped going to the grocery store because the sight of a child’s sandal in the aisle would send him into a spiral. He quit his job as a nanny entirely, telling the Okadas he was moving to the mainland. Instead, he stayed in his one-bedroom apartment, avoiding the park, the beach, the sound of children playing in the street.

He had come to believe that he should have protected Malia and that he had failed. This belief did not fade; it hardened. When he heard a neighbor mention losing a loved one, he would feel the weight of his own failure press down on him, and he would retreat further. He stopped answering phone calls from his ex-wife, stopped attending family dinners, stopped talking to anyone who might ask how he was doing. The only thing that grew was the certainty that he was a weak person, and that weakness had cost a child her life. He was convinced that if he had been stronger, faster, better, he would have reached her in time.

What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday morning in February, when he realized he had not left his apartment in eleven days. He had run out of food, and the thought of walking past the park to the corner store made his hands shake so badly he could not hold a glass of water. He sat on the edge of his bed, staring at the wall, and for the first time in three years, he wondered if there was any way back. He was terrified that therapy would only prove what he already knew—that he was beyond help—but he was more terrified of staying in that room, with the sound of a mother’s wail playing on a loop in his head, for the rest of his life.
